She was formerly an executive at a software company but had to retire due to frequent memory lapses. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 135/91 mmHg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 12/min. A 69-year-old woman presents with pain in her hip and groin. A 17-year-old boy was referred from the general practitioner to the local psychosis early-detection clinic owing to a drop in functioning and social withdrawal during the previous 6 months. He never acted on these thoughts. He reported that he no longer enjoyed his former interests and could not relate to people at college or to friends, but there were no clear signs of depressive disorders. The Structured Clinical Interview for DSM did not reveal any mental disorder.Discharge to general practitioner with no clinical recommendationsClinical follow-up for at least 3 years and indicated primary prevention. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 112/71 mmHg, pulse is 73/min, and respirations are 14/min. A 46-year-old man presents with his wife to his primary care provider for depression and strange movements. On physical exam, the patient has a flat affect with a facial grimace and sudden jerky movements of his upper extremities. He drinks a few glasses of wine per week and has never smoked. His wife reports that her husband has not been himself for the last 2 months. His wife says that he is getting worse. He is a partner at an accounting firm, but his colleagues are threatening to fire him if he continues to perform poorly at work. The patient cannot explain the recent changes to his mood and tearfully admits he fears there is something seriously wrong with him. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 141/87 mmHg, pulse is 81/min, and respirations are 12/min. His family history is unknown as he was adopted. Whereas he was previously outgoing and “the life of the party,” the patient is now irritable and withdrawn. The patient met his mother once and never knew his father but was told he died in his 50s. The patient’s medical history is significant for hypertension, for which he takes lisinopril.

A 36-year-old woman, G1P1001, presents to her gynecologist for an annual visit. A transvaginal ultrasound is performed and demonstrates two intramural leiomyomas. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 147/91 mmHg, pulse is 62/min, and respirations are 12/min. On physical exam, he appears to be in moderate distress and has pain with neck flexion. His neurological exam is within normal limits. He admits to occasional cocaine and marijuana use. The patient is certain that his neighbors have been tampering with his food and potentially poisoned him. The patient states that when he left for work this morning he was certain that he had closed the door to his pantry. The physician performs a physical exam and tells the patient that he thinks there is nothing to be concerned about, but that he should call him or come into the office if he experiences any symptoms. A 27-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for exposure to toxic materials. Upon returning home, he saw that the door to his pantry was wide open. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 115/71 mmHg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 12/min. He storms out of the office angrily, stating that he deserves the best in medical care. He also reports tearing of the left eye during these episodes. He reports that he has headaches at night several times a week. Every few weeks she has an episode of a right-sided, throbbing headache. The episodes began several years ago and are accompanied by nausea and bright spots in her vision. The headache usually subsides if she lies still in a dark, quiet room for several hours. A CT of the head is performed and shows no acute abnormalities. She works as a receptionist at a marketing company. The patient denies any weakness, numbness, or tingling during these episodes. She has 2 glasses of wine with dinner several nights a week and has never smoked. A 28-year-old woman presents to her primary care provider with a headache. On physical exam, the patient has no focal neurologic deficits. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 125/81 mmHg, pulse is 64/min, and respirations are 11/min.

A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department following a skiing accident. The patient lost control of his skis and collided with a tree. His medical history is significant for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, and a prior transient ischemic attack. He is difficult to arouse with a GCS of 7. His medications include atorvastatin and lisinopril. A head CT is performed and can be seen in Figure A.

Two months ago, the patient had a root canal on a left molar. A 3x4 cm non-tender mass can be palpated inferior to the angle of the left mandible. Over the past week, she has had increasing difficulty chewing her food and progressive pain in the left side of her jaw. Thick exudate is draining from an opening in the skin. Her medical history is significant for hyperlipidemia, mild intermittent asthma, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. On physical exam, there is a bluish hue to the skin on the lower left side of the patient’s face.

On exam, the patient is an obese girl who is clutching her head with the light in the room turned off. A 17-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a headache. A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency room reporting sudden-onset abdominal and back pain that began 3 hours ago. Intravenous fluid boluses are administered. He describes the pain as in his buttocks but states that at times it travels down his leg. He states that it feels electrical and burning in nature. A 69-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with hip and back pain. The patient has a medical history of obesity, diabetes, depression, anxiety, diverticulosis, constipation, and a surgical repair of his anterior cruciate ligament. He states this weekend he had a barbecue. On physical exam, he is found to have an intact motor and sensory function in his lower extremities bilaterally.

He has tried going to bed early for the past month but is unable to fall asleep until 2 hours prior to his alarm. A 25-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for trouble with focus and concentration. He states that he lives at home with his parents his entire life and recently was able to get a job at a local factory. A physical exam is within normal limits. The patient fears that if this continues he will lose his job. The patient states that he feels fatigued all the time and sometimes will suddenly fall asleep while operating equipment. His boss often observes him "daydreaming" with a blank stare off into space. He is unable to stay focused on any task. His boss will have to yell at him to startle him back to work. Ever since the patient started working, he has had trouble focusing on his job. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 112/68 mmHg, pulse is 81/min, and respirations are 12/min.

The lesions were warm and indurated but nontender to palpation. Lesional skin biopsies were performed (Figure 1B).A, Clinical examination shows discrete erysipeloid plaques on the anterior chest. . In 2014, she developed axillary lymphadenopathy on the right side and was found to have metastatic disease. A 65-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for a routine appointment. We compared the effect of clopidogrel plus aspirin vs aspirin alone on functional outcome and quality of life in the Clopidogrel in High-risk Patients with Acute Non-disabling Cerebrovascular Events (CHANCE) trial of aspirin-clopidogrel vs aspirin alone after acute minor stroke or TIA. Poor functional outcome occurred in 254 patients (9.9%) in the clopidogrel-aspirin group, as compared with 299 (11.6%) in the aspirin group (p = 0.046). #### **RESULTS****:** #### **OBJECTIVE****:** This study provides Class II evidence that for patients with acute minor stroke or TIA, clopidogrel plus aspirin compared to aspirin alone improves 90-day functional outcome (absolute reduction of poor outcome 1.70%, 95% confidence interval 0.03%-3.42%). #### **CLASSIFICATION** **OF** **EVIDENCE****:** Disabling stroke at 90 days occurred in 166 (6.5%) in the clopidogrel-aspirin group and in 219 (8.5%) in the aspirin group (p = 0.01). In stratified analysis by subsequent stroke, there was no difference in 90-day functional outcome and quality of life between the 2 groups. #### **CONCLUSIONS****:** In patients with minor stroke or TIA, the combination of clopidogrel and aspirin appears to be superior to aspirin alone in improving the 90-day functional outcome, and this is consistent with a reduction in the rate of disabling stroke in the dual antiplatelet arm. Poor functional outcome was defined as mRS score of 2-6 at 90 days and poor quality of life as EQ-5D index score of 0.5 or less. Poor quality of life occurred in 142 (5.5%) in the clopidogrel-aspirin group and in 175 (6.8%) in the aspirin group (p = 0.06). #### **METHODS****:** Participants were assessed at 90 days for functional outcome using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and quality of life using the EuroQol-5 Dimension (EQ-5D).

Participants were randomly assigned to continue usual care alone (guideline based, including pulmonary rehabilitation and bronchodilators; n = 157) vs usual care plus bilateral coil treatment (n = 158) involving 2 sequential procedures 4 months apart in which 10 to 14 coils were bronchoscopically placed in a single lobe of each lung. #### **CONCLUSIONS** **AND** **RELEVANCE****:** Among patients with emphysema and severe hyperinflation treated for 12 months, the use of endobronchial coils compared with usual care resulted in an improvement in median exercise tolerance that was modest and of uncertain clinical importance, with a higher likelihood of major complications. Further follow-up is needed to assess long-term effects on health outcomes. The between-group difference in median change in FEV1 was 7.0% (97.5% CI, 3.4% to ∞; 1-sided P < .001), and the between-group St George's Respiratory Questionnaire score improved -8.9 points (97.5% CI, -∞ to -6.3 points; 1-sided P < .001), each favoring the coil group. Other serious adverse events including pneumonia (20% coil vs 4.5% usual care) and pneumothorax (9.7% vs 0.6%, respectively) occurred more frequently in the coil group. #### **RESULTS****:** Among 315 participants (mean age, 64 years; 52% women), 90% completed the 12-month follow-up. Secondary end points included the difference between groups in 6-minute walk distance responder rate, absolute change in quality of life using the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire (MCID, 4) and change in forced expiratory volume in the first second (FEV1; MCID, 10%). Median change in 6-minute walk distance at 12 months was 10.3 m with coil treatment vs -7.6 m with usual care, with a between-group difference of 14.6 m (Hodges-Lehmann 97.5% CI, 0.4 m to ∞; 1-sided P = .02). Randomized clinical trial conducted among 315 patients with emphysema and severe air trapping recruited from 21 North American and 5 European sites from December 2012 through November 2015. #### **DESIGN****,** **SETTING****,** **AND** **PARTICIPANTS****:** #### **INTERVENTIONS****:** #### **MAIN** **OUTCOMES** **AND** **MEASURES****:** The primary effectiveness outcome was difference in absolute change in 6-minute-walk distance between baseline and 12 months (minimal clinically important difference [MCID], 25 m). Major complications (including pneumonia requiring hospitalization and other potentially life-threatening or fatal events) occurred in 34.8% of coil participants vs 19.1% of usual care (P = .002). He takes fluoxetine, lisinopril, and metformin every day. A 50-year-old man presents to the emergency department reporting chest pain and drooling that started immediately after eating a steak.

An internist observes multiple cases of asymptomatic hyponatremia among their ward patients. The physician considers modifying the diagnostic threshold for severe hyponatremia to < 115 mEq/L. While severe hyponatremia (traditionally defined as sodium < 120 mEq/L) typically presents with altered mental status, seizures, and coma requiring hypertonic saline treatment, the physician notes that some patients remain asymptomatic despite chronic sodium levels below 120 mEq/L.

One hundred men undergo biopsy procedures; 90 are found to have prostate cancer, and five are found to have chronic prostatitis. A needle biopsy of the prostate gland is done on all men with serum prostate-specific antigen concentrations greater than 5 ng/mL (N<4). A new blood test to detect prostate cancer is evaluated in 300 male volunteers.

He is polite to the physician but berates the nurses and other staff. The patient says with disgust that the missing child is and always has been worthless. The patient's wife and two of his three adult children arrive for a visit. A 55-year-old man who is a business executive is admitted to the hospital for evaluation of abdominal pain.

A previously healthy 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of episodes of severe anxiety, shortness of breath, palpitations, and numbness in her hands and feet. Thyroid function studies and an ECG show no abnormalities. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities.

It is hypothesized that the stress of studying for examinations adversely affects the immune system, making the students more susceptible to infection. Results show an increased incidence of upper respiratory tract infections among these students during finals week. An investigator is studying the incidence of the common cold among medical students at various time points during the school year.

A 30-year-old nulliparous female presents to the office with the complaint of mood changes. She says that for the past several months she has been anxious, hyperactive, and unable to sleep 3 to 4 days prior to the onset of menses. She further reports that on the day her menses begins she becomes acutely depressed, anorectic, irritable, and lethargic. History reveals a tuboplasty approximately 1 year ago to correct a closed fallopian tube. Physical examination findings are normal. She has no psychiatric history. She and her husband have been trying to conceive for over 2 years.

Pelvic examination shows erythema of the vulva and vagina and a thick white vaginal discharge. The pH of the discharge is 4. Two weeks ago, she had streptococcal pharyngitis treated with amoxicillin. A 19-year-old college student comes to the physician because of vaginal irritation and pain with urination for 5 days. Her last menstrual period was 1 week ago. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. She has been sexually active with two partners over the past year; she uses condoms for contraception.

He has had three similar episodes of urethritis over the past 2 years. A sexually active 23-year-old man with multiple sex partners has dysuria and a yellow urethral exudate. Gram stain of the exudate shows numerous neutrophils, many that contain intracellular gram-negative diplococci.

A 54-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of severe jaw pain since undergoing a painful dental procedure 1 day ago. Other members of her family also have experienced poor pain control with codeine. The patient was prescribed codeine after the procedure and instructed to take the medication every 4 hours, but she has continued pain despite adherence to this analgesic regimen.

S2 is widely split and does not vary with respiration. A soft mid-diastolic murmur is heard along the lower left sternal border. A healthy 4-year-old girl is brought for a well-child examination. Examination shows no other abnormalities. A grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur is heard along the upper left sternal border.

The full-field electroretinogram was nonrecordable under both scotopic and photopic conditions.A, Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) reveals extensive and diffuse retinal thinning (arrowhead) beyond the fovea, with loss of photoreceptors and pigment migration into the retina. A woman in her 70s and of Korean descent reported difficulty seeing in dimly lit settings for the past 6 years and was referred for evaluation. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography showed complete loss of photoreceptors outside the fovea, with retinal pigment epithelial atrophy, irregular proliferation, and some remodeling (Figure, A). Ophthalmoscopic examination revealed bilateral pigment mottling with extensive peripheral depigmentation of the retinal pigment epithelium, sparing the central fovea bilaterally. On examination, the best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/25 OS. . Slitlamp examination showed prominent nuclear sclerosis and a posterior subcapsular cataract in the right eye and a well-positioned intraocular lens in the left eye. Central vision with the I-4-e isopter was constricted to 5° to 7°. B, Fundus autofluorescence of the left eye shows a perimacular ring of hypofluorescence (blue asterisk) and hyperfluorescence (black asterisk) in a bull’s-eye configuration with diffuse scattered granular areas. C, Goldmann visual field of the left eye shows an evolving ring scotoma (asterisk) and a small preserved central island of vision (arrowhead). Goldmann perimetry of both eyes (Figure, C) revealed significant constriction of the V-4-e isopter with an extensive ring scotoma between approximately 10° and 30° eccentricity. Her medical history was remarkable for long-standing hypertension, diabetes, and mixed connective tissue disease. A multifocal electroretinogram (ERG) showed profound signal attenuation throughout the examined area. Fundus autofluorescence showed a ring of parafoveal hypofluorescence and hyperfluorescence, with speckled hypofluorescence peripherally (Figure, B).

A 75-year-old woman comes to the office because she has band-like, burning pain in her right upper abdomen extending from the epigastrium around to the midline of the back. Physical examination discloses no abdominal tenderness to palpation. Findings on ultrasonography of the gallbladder are normal. Serum amylase concentration is within the reference range.

A 36-year-old man comes to the office because of headaches that began 2 weeks ago. The headaches are moderately severe, are present when he awakens in the morning, and are relieved with over-the-counter analgesics. Physical examination now discloses no abnormalities except for blurring of the optic disc margins bilaterally. He has no prior history of headaches. He tells you he was promoted to an upper-level managerial position in his accounting firm about 8 months ago, which necessitated relocating.

Breast and pubic hair development are Tanner stage 5. Menarche occurred at the age of 14 years. A 15-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of acne. Physical examination shows scattered open and closed comedones over the cheeks and forehead. Breast and pubic hair development began at the age of 12 years.

Physical examination discloses tenderness over the left maxillary sinus without purulent drainage. Left frontal sinus does not transilluminate. A 19-year-old Asian female college student comes to the university health center because of a 1-week history of nasal stuffiness, occasional clear rhinorrhea, and a mild sore throat. Vital signs are temperature 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse 88/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 116/74 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination discloses no abnormalities. Medical history is unremarkable and her only medication is an oral contraceptive. BMI is 22 kg/m2 . Two days ago, she began to feel hot, but she has not taken her temperature. She has no history of allergies. There is clear fluid behind the left tympanic membrane, enlarged tonsils bilaterally, and pain with tapping of the left upper incisors. She does not smoke cigarettes.

The investigators defined antihypertensive therapy as effective if the treatment resulted in a blood pressure measurement below 140/90 mm Hg. Study participants include 140 women (70%) and 60 men (30%) ages 30 to 60 years, with baseline blood pressure measurements of 150/95 mm Hg or higher. When designing the study, the investigators set the probability of wrongly finding that Drug X is more effective than the standard therapy as 1%; they set the probability of wrongly finding that the effectiveness of the two drugs is the same as 10%. A randomized controlled trial is conducted to assess the effectiveness of a new combination-drug antihypertensive therapy (Drug X) compared with a standard antihypertensive single-drug therapy.

He had an anterior myocardial infarction 3 years ago and has had shortness of breath with mild exertion since then. Current medications include labetalol and daily aspirin. A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of progressive fatigue and ankle swelling. Crackles are heard at both lung bases. Cardiac examination shows an S3 gallop. There is edema from the midtibia to the ankle bilaterally. There are jugular venous pulsations 5 cm above the sternal angle. His pulse is 100/min and regular, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 130/75 mm Hg. He has smoked one-half pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years.

She has hypertension treated with enalapril for the past 3 months. Examination and an x-ray of the chest show no abnormalities. She does not smoke. There is no history of lung disease. A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of persistent nonproductive cough for 6 weeks. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, pulse is 70/min, and respirations are 12/min. She has not had fever or weight loss. She weighs 54 kg (120 lb) and is 163 cm (64 in) tall.

She says that his teachers reprimand him frequently for running wildly in the classroom, talking excessively, and getting out of his seat; he often forgets to turn in his homework. His mother says that he is extremely active and likes to climb. A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after injuring his arm when he fell out of a tree. Mental status examination shows a neutral affect. He says that he likes to run and climb trees. The patient is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. His pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 100/80 mm Hg. During the past year, he fractured his right tibia after falling off a trampoline and sustained a concussion after falling off his bicycle. Physical examination shows a dislocated left shoulder, healing abrasions over the elbows, and ecchymoses in various stages of healing over the knees. His father has a history of illicit drug use. His parents are currently divorcing.

Palpation of the left lower extremity discloses a strong femoral pulse, a weak popliteal pulse, and a cool, pulseless foot. The left lower extremity and foot appear pale. A 49-year-old man, who is recovering in the hospital 2 days after uncomplicated left femoral-popliteal bypass grafting for claudication, has now developed increasing pain in his left foot. The surgical incision appears clean and well approximated without abnormal erythema or swelling. Medical history is remarkable for type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled with metformin and diet. Until now, the patient's postoperative course had been unremarkable and he has been treated with low-dose morphine for pain control. Vital signs now are temperature 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse 80/min and regular, respirations 20/min, and blood pressure 150/92 mm Hg.

Examination of the skin shows a purple-red discoloration over the cheeks and eyelids, periorbital edema, erythematous plaques and scales over the elbows and knees, and flat-topped red papules over all knuckles. A 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of progressive weakness and a purple-red discoloration over his cheeks and upper eyelids over the past 8 weeks. There is generalized weakness and atrophy of the proximal muscles. He is at the 75th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight; he has had no change in his weight since his last examination 9 months ago. His only medication is a topical corticosteroid for several dry, scaly patches of the skin. His mother says that she was careful to apply his sunscreen on the trip and can recall no tick bites or exposure to poisonous plants. His symptoms began shortly after a camping trip, and he now is unable to climb stairs, walk long distances, comb his hair, or dress himself. His temperature is 37.7°C (99.8°F), blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg, pulse is 105/min, and respirations are 28/min. He appears weak and lethargic.

The lesions started spontaneously as erythematous tender papules with white purulent discharge. Fungal and bacterial culture samples were negative. Rheumatoid factor was elevated at 198 IU/mL, and other laboratory data were noncontributory. B, Left pretibia at 7-day follow-up. He reported a medical history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic kidney disease, and heavy tobacco use. The limb was dusky with scattered hyperpigmented patches and surrounding erythema (Figure, A and B). The patient denied any recent changes to his medications or recent travel. Both lower limbs exhibited pitting edema of 1+ severity, and negative Homans sign bilaterally for deep vein thrombosis. A punch biopsy specimen was obtained from the edge of the lesion (Figure, C and D).A, Left pretibia on initial visit. C, Periodic acid–Schiff stain (original magnification ×4). . D, Hematoxylin-eosin stain (original magnification ×20). He recently failed a course of amoxicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethaxazole initiated by his primary care physician. A man in his 50s presented with a 2-month medical history of painful, gradually expanding ulcers on the left lower leg. No other household members were affected.Physical examination of the left lower extremity revealed a 2.5-cm keratotic plaque with central ulceration that expressed a straw-colored fluid.

Examination shows a vulvar pustule that has ulcerated and formed multiple satellite lesions. A smear of fluid from the lesions establishes the diagnosis. Nodes are palpated in the inguinal and femoral areas. A sexually active 20-year-old woman has had fever, chills, malaise, and pain of the vulva for 2 days.

Physical examination shows areflexia. A 64-year-old man with non-Hodgkin lymphoma comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of progressive numbness in his hands and feet and weakness in his legs when he stands. He received his third course of chemotherapy 4 weeks ago.

His wife says that he has always snored loudly, and over the past year, he has had episodes of choking or gasping for breath while sleeping. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 105 kg (231 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m2 . Physical and neurologic examinations show no other abnormalities. A 52-year-old man comes to the physician with his wife because of a 1-year history of excessive daytime sleepiness. He also once fell asleep while driving at night and drove off the road, narrowly avoiding injury. His pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 150/76 mm Hg. He does not think the symptoms are problematic, but his wife is concerned because he sometimes falls asleep on the sofa early in the evening when guests are present.

A grade 3/6, diastolic blowing murmur is heard over the left sternal border and radiates to the right sternal border. Femoral pulses are decreased bilaterally. His pulse is 110/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 110/50 mm Hg. He has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. An ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy. A 47-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of shortness of breath, severe chest pain, and sweating. He has no history of similar symptoms.

Shortly after administration of the influenza virus vaccine, she develops shortness of breath, hives, and angioedema. A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician for her first influenza virus vaccination. She has a history of untreated hypertension. Her blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg, and pulse is 100/min.

A 42-year-old woman with a history of multiple sclerosis comes to the office because she had a sudden loss of vision in the right eye. External ocular movements are normal but funduscopic examination shows pallor of the optic disk. She has no history of diplopia.

Pelvic examination shows a purulent cervical discharge, cervical motion tenderness, and bilateral adnexal tenderness. A previously healthy 17-year-old girl comes to the emergency department because of a 5-day history of progressive lower abdominal pain, fever, and malodorous vaginal discharge. Abdominal examination shows severe lower quadrant tenderness bilaterally. She is sexually active with one male partner and uses a combination contraceptive patch. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Menarche was at the age of 12 years, and her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. Her hemoglobin concentration is 10.5 g/dL, leukocyte count is 13,000/mm3 , and platelet count is 345,000/mm3 . A urine pregnancy test is negative.

Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows a 2-cm ectopic pregnancy in the ampulla. A 26-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of an 8-hour history of severe back and abdominal pain and mild but persistent vaginal bleeding. The ampulla has ruptured into the surrounding tissue.

She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the past 20 years. She has a family history of early coronary artery disease (CAD) and her father died suddenly at age 46 years of myocardial infarction. She tells you that she has never had chest pain. She exercises two or three times a week for about 20 minutes on a treadmill. Her only medication is acetaminophen for tension headaches. A 36-year-old female advertising executive is referred to the office for evaluation of a fasting serum total cholesterol concentration of 249 mg/dL. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities except for mild obesity. She is not currently sexually active and has no children. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 76 kg (167 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m2 . She claims that her high-stress lifestyle makes it impossible for her to eat regular meals or to follow a special diet, and she usually eats fast food. Vital signs today are normal.

The cervix is friable with a 1-cm exophytic mass lateral to the cervical os at the nine o'clock position. A 39-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the community-based health center because of a 6-month history of a copious, foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She also reports spotting that began 6 months ago and has progressed to heavy bleeding during the past 3 weeks. Medical history is significant for an abnormal Pap smear in her 20s; her most recent Pap smear was done 12 years ago during her second pregnancy, and she recalls the results as being normal. She takes no medications. Vital signs are temperature 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse 90/min, respirations 14/min, and blood pressure 155/96 mm Hg. Speculum examination discloses normal vaginal mucosa. BMI is 32 kg/m2 . The patient was married for 18 years; her husband died 4 years ago and had undergone vasectomy after the birth of their last child. The patient has not had any new sexual partners since her husband's death.

Testing for herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus were also ordered.A, Scattered vesicles with an erythematous base on the lower back. A female infant with relapsed refractory infantile acute lymphoblastic leukemia, blast crisis (>60% blasts), and central nervous system involvement was admitted for reinduction chemotherapy with cytarabine, vincristine, daunorubicin, methotrexate, and dexamethasone. Seventeen days after her last day of chemotherapy, while neutropenic, she became febrile and developed several vesicles with an erythematous base on the lower back (Figure, A) and left thigh. Tissue and blood cultures and a punch biopsy specimen of a vesicle on the lower back were obtained. C, Hematoxylin and eosin stain (original magnification ×600). B, Hematoxylin and eosin stain (original magnification ×200). D, Gram stain (original magnification ×600). . Hematoxylin-eosin (Figures, B and C), gram (Figure, D), and periodic acid-Schiff stains were performed on the punch biopsy.

Examination reveals exophthalmos, inflammation of the periorbital tissue and conjunctivae, a heart rate of 140/min, and warm, velvety skin. A 43-year-old female presents to the office with a 2-month history of heat intolerance, weight loss, tachycardia, and diffuse goiter.

Past medical history is unremarkable, and he takes no medications. He denies any trauma, recent upper respiratory illness, or history of prior bloody nose. A 64-year-old male presents to the emergency room with a bloody nose that has been dripping out his nares for the past 2 hours. Examination of the nasal passages reveals that the site of the bleeding is on the septal mucosa of the right naris. He has a blood pressure of 180/90 mmHg.

Physical examination shows lesions that are most numerous in the flexural areas including the axillae and groin. A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of recurrent, widespread blister formation. The blisters do not break easily, and there are no oral lesions.

Examination shows anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, nonexudative conjunctivitis bilaterally, a strawberry tongue, an erythematous truncal rash, and edema of the hands and feet. A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of temperatures to 39.4°C (102.9°F) for 8 days.

A 40-year-old female secretary comes to the office because of a 2-month history of fatigue, and generalized aching and weakness of the proximal muscles of all four extremities. The patient initially noticed the weakness only while she was getting in and out of her car, but during the past 2 weeks, the weakness has progressed, so that she now has difficulty combing her hair. Results of serum laboratory studies show a creatine kinase concentration of 600 U/L and a lactate dehydrogenase concentration of 800 U/L. Vital signs are temperature 37.7°C (99.8°F), pulse 90/min, respirations 20/min, and blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg. The patient is alert and fully oriented. She is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 68 kg(150 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m2 . She appears uncomfortable. The muscles of the upper arms and legs are somewhat tender to pressure. She was adopted and family history is unknown. Physical examination discloses cracking of the skin of both hands that involves the tips and lateral sides of several fingers. Since the symptoms began, she also has had aching of the joints in her hands that has responded partially to ibuprofen. She has two teenaged children who are well. Results of complete blood count are within the reference ranges.

He denies any trauma. A 16-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with sudden-onset swelling of the right knee. Past medical history reveals cystic fibrosis. Numerous bruises are noted in various stages of resolution. Further history reveals easy bruising and bleeding from the gums over the past month. Examination of the knee reveals fluctuance on palpation of the joint but no increased warmth; mild restriction in range of motion due to the swelling is also noted.

There is a 1-cm area of erythema over the sacrum with intact skin and no induration. Neurologic examination shows quadriparesis. A 65-year-old man who is quadriplegic as a result of multiple sclerosis is hospitalized for treatment of left lower lobe pneumonia. He appears malnourished. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.5°F), pulse is 95/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Examination of the heart, lymph nodes, abdomen, and extremities shows no abnormalities. Rhonchi are heard at the left lower lobe of the lung on auscultation.

Her father had classic hemophilia. A karyotype obtained from an amniotic fluid sample of the patient shows that the fetus is XY. A 25-year-old woman who is 19 weeks pregnant comes to the office for a prenatal examination.

A 20-year-old female presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of nausea and vomiting. She is a pre-med college student and admits to being under a lot of stress as she takes final exams. She says that today she noticed a slight amount of blood in her vomit. She also says that she drinks a large amount of coffee daily. Vital signs are normal.

Twelve hours after the operation he develops circumoral numbness and paresthesias in his fingertips, and he becomes very anxious. A 60-year-old man had a total thyroidectomy and excision of enlarged left jugular lymph nodes for follicular carcinoma. Physical examination discloses a dry neck dressing and no stridor. He is receiving intravenous 5% dextrose and 0.45% saline with potassium. Extremities are warm, with brisk capillary refill time. Vital signs are temperature 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse 90/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 140/90 mm Hg. The operation was uncomplicated.

Moderate amount of Elschnig pearls (most pronounced on the left of the asterisks).Perform pars plana vitrectomy with removal of intraocular lens and capsular bag plus intravitreal antibiotics. IOP was 24 mm Hg in the right eye and 18 mm Hg in the left eye.Slitlamp examination revealed a milky substance in the retrolental space, more pronounced in the right eye (Figure) but evident in both. Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 1.0 and 0.5 (Snellen equivalent, 20/20 and 20/40) OD and OS, respectively. His manifest refraction revealed a difference of −0.75 D sphere compared with his own preexisting glasses in the right eye. A 78-year-old White man was referred to our clinic for evaluation of an unexplained subjective decrease in vision for more than 6 months, more pronounced in the right eye, and insufficiently controlled intraocular pressure (IOP). Local antiglaucoma therapy with a fixed-combination prostaglandin and β-blocker was used regularly in both eyes owing to long-standing primary open-angle glaucoma. Uneventful cataract surgery with phacoemulsification and in-the-bag insertion of an intraocular lens was performed 10 years earlier in both eyes. The rest of the slitlamp examination was unremarkable with moderate superficial punctate keratitis owing to ocular surface disease, an anterior chamber depth of Van Herick grade 4 (peripheral anterior chamber depth >1 corneal thickness), an absence of anterior chamber inflammation, and a moderate amount of Elschnig pearls in both eyes.Right eye with milky-opaque substance (between white arrowheads) in the retrolental space and distension of the capsular bag.

A 65-year-old man who had been treated for hypertension for the past 10 years presented with increasing fatigue, dizziness, and palpitations. An electrocardiogram (ECG) was obtained (Figure 1).Review the ECG for frequent atrial ectopic beatsReview the ECG for features of atrial fibrillationReview the ECG for atrial flutter with varying AV blockReview the ECG for features of multifocal atrial tachycardia. He did not have chest pain or any other symptoms.
In a cohort study of elderly women, the relative risk ratio for hip fractures among those who exercise regularly is 1.2 (95% confidence interval of 1.1 to 1.8).

A 33-year-old man undergoes a radical thyroidectomy for thyroid cancer. Postoperatively, serum studies show a calcium concentration of 7.5 mg/dL, albumin concentration of 4 g/dL, and parathyroid hormone concentration of 200 pg/mL. During the operation, moderate hemorrhaging requires ligation of several vessels in the left side of the neck.

Review of her medical records confirms that the initial diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis is correct. A 44-year-old woman with a 10-year history of arthritis comes to the office because she has had increasing pain and stiffness in her hands, wrists, and knees during the past several months. There is moderate ulnar deviation of the fingers. She also has had increasing fatigue for the past month, along with a weight loss of 1.8 to 2.2 kg (4 to 5 lb). She characterizes these attacks as episodes of weakness and loss of feeling in her legs for several minutes. During one of these episodes, she became incontinent. She has seen numerous physicians for her arthritis in the past and has tried various medications and devices, including copper bracelets from Mexico given to her by friends. Physical examination shows facial plethora and swollen and painful metacarpophalangeal and knee joints, bilaterally. She says, "I had several drop attacks during the past 3 months." She currently takes aspirin approximately four times daily and ibuprofen occasionally. The remainder of the examination discloses no abnormalities.

Three days after hospitalization for diabetic ketoacidosis, an 87-year-old woman refuses insulin injections. She accurately describes her medical history and understands the consequences of refusing insulin. She says that her medical condition has declined so much that she no longer wishes to go on living; she is nearly blind and will likely require bilateral leg amputations. There is no evidence of depression. She has no family and most of her friends are sick or deceased. She dismisses any attempts by the physician to change her mind, saying that the physician is too young to understand her situation. On mental status examination, she is alert and cooperative. She reports that she has always been an active person and does not see how her life will be of value anymore.

Physical examination shows conjunctival injection and discharge and oropharyngeal erythema. An 8-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother because of a 3-day history of fever, sore throat, and itchy eyes. He just returned from a weeklong summer camp that included hiking trips and swimming lessons in the camp-owned swimming pool. The public health department reports an outbreak of similar symptoms among the other campers and camp volunteers. He has no history of major medical illness and receives no medications. His temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F); other vital signs are within normal limits. He appears tired.

Vital signs are temperature 36.0°C (96.8°F), pulse 110/min, respirations 12/min, and blood pressure 90/50 mm Hg. He drinks eight to ten alcoholic beverages daily. A 37-year-old man comes to the emergency department because he has felt nauseated and light-headed for the past hour. Medical history is significant for esophageal varices secondary to alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites treated with spironolactone. While you are obtaining additional history, the patient vomits a large volume of bright red blood and becomes difficult to arouse.

He is sitting upright and appears catatonic. Physical examination shows rigidity. During the examination, he becomes hostile and attempts to assault the physician. A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after being found with a "blank stare" and flat facial expression at a party. His pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 104/68 mm Hg.

She says she is anxious about flying and even slightly "panicky." A 24-year-old recent college graduate comes to the office because of a 3-year history of increased frequency of urination and occasional incontinence whenever she travels. She reports having had similar but milder symptoms prior to examinations before graduating. Her only medication is an oral contraceptive. Vital signs are normal. She says the urinary symptoms typically begin a few days before she is going to fly and they stop the day after she arrives at her destination. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Urinalysis and urine culture are normal. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable.

On physical examination, she has mild bowlegs (10-degree genu varum). The child was weaned at 6 months of age and began to walk at 10 months of age. A healthy 2-year-old girl is brought to the office for a routine well-child visit.

An ECG shows a P-wave rate of 90/min, and an R-wave rate of 40/min, with no apparent relation between the two. A 54-year-old man comes to the physician because of episodes of fainting for 3 months. Physical examination shows evidence of cannon a waves. His pulse is 40/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 138/85 mm Hg. He had a myocardial infarction 12 years ago. He also has had difficulty performing daily tasks because he is easily fatigued.

Two days later he noticed a maculopapular rash on his neck and trunk, which later involved his upper and lower extremities. He did not smoke and only drank alcohol occasionally. A previously healthy man in his 30s presented with a 5-day history of fever, anorexia, and rash. A maculopapular rash was noted on the trunk and extremities (Figure) as well as the palms and soles. There was no neck stiffness or lymphadenopathy. He was alert and oriented. Serum electrolyte levels were normal. . The lungs were clear to auscultation. Neurologic examination, including results of motor, sensory, and reflex testing, was unremarkable. The face was not involved. He was living in Japan and recently visited a neighboring island but denied any international travel.On examination, his blood pressure was 142/84 mm Hg; temperature, 38.3°C; pulse, 91/min; respiratory rate, 24/min; and oxygen saturation, 97% on ambient air. Aspartate aminotransferase level was 635 U/L (10.6 μkat/L); alanine aminotransferase (ALT), 491 U/L (8.2 μkat/L); lactate dehydrogenase, 807 U/L (13.48 μkat/L); γ-glutamyltransferase, 329 U/L (5.49 μkat/L); and bilirubin, 1.3 mg/dL (22.24 μmol/L). Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 2900/μL (80% neutrophils, 13% lymphocytes, 6% monocytes, 0% eosinophils, and 0% basophils); hemoglobin level, 15.2 g/dL; and platelet count, 187 ×103/μL. Five days before arrival, he developed throat pain, rhinorrhea, nonproductive cough, and fever. There were no mucosal lesions or conjunctival injection. No hepatosplenomegaly was noted.

The student met the woman when he was assigned to her care during her 2-week hospitalization for treatment of major depressive disorder. A 22-year-old woman contacts a medical student and asks if he would like to join her for dinner. He has not treated or seen the patient since she was discharged from the hospital. He is attracted to this former patient and would be interested in dating her.

Her blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 100/min. A 45-year-old woman has a 2-week history of increased anxiety, abdominal discomfort, irritability, and difficulty concentrating; she was robbed at knifepoint in a parking lot 3 weeks ago. She is cooperative but appears anxious, glancing around quickly when a loud noise is heard outside the office. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Examination shows dry skin and hair. She takes levothyroxine for hypothyroidism and uses an over-the-counter inhaler as needed for exercise-induced asthma. Leukocyte count is 12,000/mm3 , and serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is 5.0 μU/mL.

Medical history is remarkable for gestational diabetes mellitus during her pregnancies. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 37 kg/m2 . She takes no medications except for an oral contraceptive. Vital signs are normal, and physical examination discloses no abnormalities. However, the pain seems to recur every 2 to 3 months. She walks 3 miles daily for exercise and works as a sales representative for a computer software company. A 29-year-old Hispanic woman, gravida 3, para 3, comes to the office because of recurrent low back pain during the past year. Rest and analgesics usually eradicate the pain within 2 weeks.

Her mother says, "She is getting almost all A's in school and she is on the track team." She is 158 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 43 kg (95 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m2 . A 15-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because of abdominal pain and constipation for the past several weeks. Pulse is 65/min. She requests a laxative to help with her constipation. You ask the patient about her diet and she responds, "I'm kind of a picky eater."

Despite his poor control, he demands that he be discharged. Prior to admission to the hospital, his only medication was insulin, although he often missed doses. He has been avoiding his family and friends because he is not in the mood to see them but admits that he is lonely. He did not get out of bed for 2 days, which prompted his wife to call an ambulance and have him admitted to the hospital. He says that he has been noncompliant with his diabetic regimen, adding, "Sometimes I forget." There is no evidence of suicidal ideation. He is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 36 kg/m2 . On mental status examination, he is tired and has a restricted affect. Cognition is intact. His fasting serum glucose concentration is 120 mg/dL. A 37-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus is admitted to the hospital because of inadequate control of his glucose concentrations for the past 2 months. He does not drink alcohol. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 68/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 150/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. He reports that he has had a 3-month history of fatigue, irritability, and feelings of hopelessness.

A 7-month-old infant, who was recently discharged from the hospital following an episode of enteritis and dehydration, has persistent watery diarrhea. His mother feeds him cow-milk formula and a variety of strained fruits and vegetables. No other abnormalities are seen. On physical examination, his temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), his mucous membranes are dry, and his abdomen is slightly distended.

She had been having regular contractions every 4 minutes, but is now having only a few intermittent, weak contractions. Examination shows no reason for obstructed labor. The fetal head is engaged, the membranes are intact, the fetal heart tones are normal, and the cervix is 100% effaced and 7 cm dilated. A 25-year-old gravida 3 para 2 female is admitted to the hospital at 39 weeks' gestation in active labor. She has received medication for pain twice in the past 6 hours.

She has never been married and does not work or attend school. She has not had previous episodes, although for more than 1 year she has had occasional difficulty passing stools. She has no other symptoms. She is not in pain but is afraid to move her bowels for fear that the problem will worsen. A 15-year-old girl comes to the emergency department because, she says, "something has been sticking out of my bottom since I had a bowel movement this morning." She tells you that she moved away from home more than a year ago and that her parents contribute nothing to her support. She has a 6-month-old child and lives with a 28-year-old female cousin.

Microscopic examination of the urine shows pigmented granular casts and rare erythrocytes. Her serum creatine kinase activity is 10,300 U/L. Examination shows erythema, warmth, and induration of the upper back, buttocks, and posterior thighs. Urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood. Her pulse is 96/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 124/58 mm Hg. On arrival, she is unable to provide a history. A 37-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 45 minutes after she was found unconscious on her apartment floor. Urine toxicology screening is positive for opiates and cocaine. Her coworkers became concerned when she did not arrive for work.

Neck is stiff with painful flexion; when the patient's neck is flexed forward, she reports and electric shock sensation. Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light; there is mild photophobia. Examination of the head shows no abnormalities. There is no history of trauma and she takes no medications. Vital signs are temperature 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse 86/min, respirations 19/min, and blood pressure 182/100 mm Hg. A 34-year-old white woman comes to the emergency department because of a persistent dull headache for the past 3 days. She says, "I haven't slept in 3 days and I am having trouble focusing at work." A midsystolic click is heard best at the left sternal border; there are no murmurs or gallops. Examination of the lower extremities shows varicosities bilaterally and 1+ edema; muscle strength is 4/5. A serous effusion is noted on examination of the left tympanic membrane. Funduscopic examination is normal. Abdominal examination shows striae, but is otherwise noncontributory. She has been taking acetaminophen without relief. Mild expiratory wheezes are heard on auscultation of the chest. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 14 years but does not drink alcoholic beverages. Neurologic examination shows no other abnormalities.

A dilated fundus examination was notable for mild vitritis of both eyes, mild hyperemia of the right optic nerve, and a large white lesion that encompassed the nerve and macula of both eyes. showing multiple areas of hyperfluorescence in the macula and periphery with peripheral vascular leakage. Over the next 2 weeks, he experienced a rapid worsening of vision in both eyes and presented to the Illinois Eye and Ear Infirmary. His right eye had experienced an episode of blurry vision 4 months previously that had spontaneously improved over a few weeks. She has begun smoking cigarettes, disobeying her curfew, and being truant from school. Since the separation, however, she has become sullen, defiant, and rebellious. A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician after her mother learned that she began having sexual intercourse with various partners 1 month ago. The patient's parents separated 3 months ago. The mother is concerned about her behavior. She does not use condoms or other contraception. She had been an honor student and excelled in sports and leadership positions at school before the separation.

On application of a dilute solution of acetic acid, the lesions turn white. Examination shows three sessile, flesh-colored lesions on the shaft of the penis that are 10 mm in diameter. He says they have not changed in size. He occasionally smokes marijuana. He takes no medications. There is no lymphadenopathy. A previously healthy 27-year-old man comes to the physician 4 weeks after noticing three nontender lesions on his penis. He is sexually active with multiple male and female partners and uses condoms inconsistently. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F). The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. He drinks two to five beers on social occasions.

Physical examination shows delayed capillary refill of the lips and nail beds and cool extremities. A 59-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 4-day history of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. His current medication is a diuretic. He has a history of mild hypertension. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 70/47 mm Hg. His oxyhemoglobin saturation in a central vein is 60% (N=70–75). He also has been confused and agitated during this period.
A 13-month-old child is brought to the emergency department because of urticaria, swelling of the lips, and difficulty breathing immediately after eating an egg.

Following the administration of desmopressin, urine osmolality increases. Laboratory studies show a serum glucose concentration within the reference range, increased serum osmolality, and decreased urine osmolality. Two weeks later, the patient develops polyuria and polydipsia. Neurologic examination shows no other abnormalities. Physical examination shows a sluggish response to stimuli. A skull x-ray shows a linear, nondepressed basal skull fracture. A 27-year-old man is admitted to the hospital 45 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle collision.

The patient remains unable to eat 6 days after surgery. Her body mass index was 23 kg/m2 before surgery, and, except for the cholecystitis, she was in good health. A 35-year-old female develops nausea and vomiting after she underwent a cholecystectomy for protracted ileus.

Intravenous glucose is administered, and the patient's symptoms improve. The symptoms improve following ingestion of orange juice or soft drinks. She has had similar episodes over the past 6 months. Her serum glucose concentration is 30 mg/dL. Examination shows no abnormalities. A 27-year-old nurse comes to the emergency department because of nervousness, dizziness, palpitations, and excess perspiration for the past 3 hours. She says that she has had a great deal of stress. She has been drinking two alcoholic beverages daily for the past month; before this time, she seldom drank alcohol.

The pain is often triggered by cold air, chewing, tactile stimulation, and brushing her teeth. The patient cannot tolerate touch over the right side of the face. Each episode of pain lasts for 1 second or less. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 62 kg (137 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m2 . A 54-year-old woman comes to the office because she has had intermittent shooting pain over her right cheek and jaw during the past 3 weeks. She has had no trauma to the face or head. Vital signs are normal. Medical history is remarkable for tension headaches, obesity, and gastric bypass surgery. CT scan of the head with and without contrast shows no abnormalities. There is no facial weakness or loss of sensation. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities.

His insulin regimen has not changed during the past year; however, his mother says he has been only marginally compliant with his insulin and dietary regimens. A 12-year-old boy with sickle cell disease and type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the office by his mother for an initial visit. Since that time, he has been treated with insulin and dietary management. The patient's vital signs are temperature 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse 72/min, respirations 24/min, and blood pressure 110/64 mm Hg. Type 1 diabetes mellitus was diagnosed in the patient 6 years ago. Measurement of hemoglobin A1c obtained last week was 5.4%. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. His diabetic diary shows home fingerstick blood glucose concentrations ranging from 140–200 mg/dL during the past 3 months. He admits to checking his glucose concentrations infrequently. The family recently moved to the area.

She presents to the office today to ask for help in dealing with midthoracic back pain to enable her to use less analgesic agents. She has undergone both radiation and chemotherapy for metastatic carcinoma to the bone. A 68-year-old female has a history of breast cancer that has recurred twice in the past 5 years.

Ultrasound biomicroscopy confirmed the diagnosis of Peters anomaly type I with iridocorneal adhesions and no apparent lens involvement. A 4-week-old male infant presented to the pediatric ophthalmology clinic with bilateral congenital corneal opacities. His corneal abnormalities were noted by the neonatologists on the first day of life. . The pregnancy was full-term and uncomplicated, and he was delivered spontaneously without the use of forceps. A systemic survey revealed no other dysmorphic findings. He was referred to the clinic for further evaluation and management. Examination under anesthesia revealed bilateral corneal opacities with peripheral clearing and absent red reflexes.

Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Six days after treatment is started, she develops a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F). Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 100/mm3 (5% segmented neutrophils and 95% lymphocytes). A 55-year-old woman with small cell carcinoma of the lung is admitted to the hospital to undergo chemotherapy.

Examination shows a migrating serpiginous pruritic perianal rash. A 14-year-old girl has had nausea, intermittent diarrhea, and a 2.2-kg (5-lb) weight loss over the past 4 weeks. Her leukocyte count is 8000/mm3 with 20% eosinophils.

A 37-year-old Anglo-American man is admitted to the hospital for treatment for cocaine dependency. The patient is using insurance coverage through his wife but does not wish for his diagnosis to be disclosed to anyone. He did not like his hospital outpatient group but liked his single session at Cocaine Anonymous. He says he has tried repeatedly to abstain from cocaine use but lives in a part of town where there are heavy drug sales. Physical examination shows a thin man with good muscle strength and no focal neurologic deficits. Vital signs are temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse 70/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 125/85 mm Hg. There is also a warrant for his arrest for assault and battery. He is on probation after a conviction for aggravated robbery 3 years ago.

A 14-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a physical examination prior to participating in sports. Serum concentrations of gonadotropic hormones, estrogens, and testosterone are within the reference ranges. He is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. Physical examination shows bilateral 1.5-cm fibroglandular masses located beneath the nipple-areolar complex and normal penis and testes. Pubic hair development is Tanner stage 3. He appears reluctant to remove his shirt for the examination, and says that he is embarrassed because he has grown breasts during the past year.

A 37-year-old man comes to the physician because of nonradiating low back pain for 3 days. Examination of the back shows bilateral paravertebral muscle spasm. Straight-leg raising is negative. The pain began after he worked in his yard. Vital signs are within normal limits. Range of motion is limited by pain. He had one similar episode 3 years ago that resolved spontaneously. He has not had any change in bowel movements or urination.

A 29-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because she has had increasingly severe lower abdominal pain and nausea for the past 2 days. Her last menstrual period ended 6 days ago. She is sexually active and does not use any contraception. Physical examination discloses abdominal tenderness in the lower quadrants bilaterally with rebound and guarding. Pelvic examination discloses leukorrhea at the cervical os and tenderness of the uterus to palpation. Temperature is 38.3°C (101.0°F). The adnexal areas are tender but no masses are palpable.

She has a flexed posture and is unable to open her mouth wide. Passive and active range of motion of the upper extremities is full. The patient does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcoholic beverages. Family history is significant for stable angina in her father and rheumatoid arthritis in her mother. Physical examination discloses thickening and hardening of the skin over the dorsum of the hands and forearms, as well as mild kyphosis. Vital signs are normal. The patient has a 102-year-old grandmother who resides in a nursing care facility and has Parkinson disease. She is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 81 kg (179 lb); BMI is 27 kg/m2 . A 57-year-old woman comes to the office for a preoperative evaluation 2 weeks before undergoing scheduled laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable and the patient takes no medications. Gait is slow and deliberate. During the interview, her face is expressionless. The remainder of the physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Strength testing shows no abnormalities; muscle tension is normal.

Ultrasonography of the thyroid gland confirms a solid, 1-cm nodule. Physical examination shows a palpable nodule in the right lobe of the thyroid gland. Medical history is unremarkable and he takes no routine medications. The patient has been generally healthy. Vital signs are normal. Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is within the reference range. A 40-year-old man comes to the office for a preemployment physical examination.
A 2-month-old female is brought to the office for her first routine health maintenance examination and for her immunization update.

Chest x-ray shows prominent pulmonary vascular markings and fluid in the intralobar fissures. Apgar scores were 9 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 95%. Physical examination discloses mild subcostal and intercostal retractions. The neonate was born via cesarean delivery due to fetal heart rate decelerations. The infant's vital signs now are temperature 36.6°C (97.8°F), pulse 150/min, and respirations 70/min. The patient is 50 cm (20 in; 50th percentile) long and weighs 3005 g (6 lb 10 oz; 50th percentile); head circumference is 35 cm (14 in; 50th percentile). One episode of chlamydial cervicitis was detected during the last trimester and treated with azithromycin. A male neonate, who was born at 36 weeks' gestation 2 hours ago in the labor and delivery unit of the hospital, now shows signs of respiratory difficulty. The amniotic fluid was stained with light particulate meconium. The mother, an 18-year-old primigravid woman, smoked one pack of cigarettes daily throughout her pregnancy. She received prenatal care during most of the pregnancy.

There was a barely perceptible right relative afferent pupillary defect. On ophthalmoscopy, there were few vitreous cells with no detectable haze and optic nerve head edema grade IV on the Frisén scale, with peripapillary flame hemorrhages in the right eye (Figure); the optic nerve was normal on the left. Review of systems was positive for a skin rash on the upper arms and trunk, which he noticed 2 months earlier. Anterior segment examination was normal. A total of 1000 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus are enrolled. Results show that the new drug is significantly better than standard treatment. The alpha and beta values for calculating probability are 0.05 and 0.20, respectively. Patients are randomly assigned to receive the new drug or standard treatment. A study is conducted to assess the effectiveness of a new drug for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Cervical range of motion is moderately limited in all fields. A 78-year-old male presents to the office with the complaint of severe neck pain. He is treated with articulatory springing technique. He rates the pain as a 7 on a scale of 0 to 10 scale. Four hours later the physician receives a call from the local emergency department, where the patient presented confused, nauseated, and vertiginous. He denies any radicular pain or numbness. He denies any trauma but reports that he had been doing a lot of painting over the past week.

One hundred individuals who received Drug X died of a particular type of cancer and 100 individuals who did not receive the drug died of the same type of cancer. A total of 600 individuals with a specific disease were included in the trial. Of the participants, 200 individuals received Drug X and 400 individuals did not receive it. It is known that Drug X is associated with an increased probability of cancer in patients who use the drug. A physician is conducting a retrospective review of a trial involving the use of Drug X in patients with a specific disease.

She says she is frustrated by her symptoms and has stopped traveling because of her frequent, urgent need to use the bathroom. The pain is usually relieved with defecation and does not occur at night or interfere with sleep. The lower abdomen is mildly tender to palpation; there is no rebound tenderness or guarding. Antigliadin antibodies are not present. A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-year history of chronic diarrhea and intermittent, crampy, lower abdominal pain. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference ranges. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative.

In addition to their usual therapy, all children are treated with acupuncture three times a week for 2 months. Sixty children with chronic headaches are recruited for the study. A study is designed to evaluate the feasibility of acupuncture in children with chronic headaches.

Bilateral wheezing is heard on auscultation of the chest. A 17-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 15 minutes after being stung by a bee. Physical examination shows no urticaria. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. She has mild lightheadedness but no difficulty swallowing.

A loud murmur is heard on auscultation; there is a thrill. Five years after being shot in the right thigh, a 21-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a buzzing sensation adjacent to the scar. At the time of the initial wound, he was discharged after 6 hours of observation with no fractures or soft-tissue swelling. He has dilated varicose veins with incompetent valves in the lower leg.

The pain is relieved with sitting up and leaning forward. A previously healthy 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of constant substernal chest pain for 12 hours that is exacerbated by coughing and inspiration. An ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevation in all leads. Cardiac examination shows distant heart sounds. An x-ray of the chest shows normal findings. There is no family history of heart disease. The lungs are clear to auscultation. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 120/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg.

A 24-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-day history of a red, itchy rash on his buttocks and legs. Physical examination shows the findings in the photograph. He appears well. Four days ago, he returned from a cruise to the Caribbean, during which he swam in the ship’s pool and used the hot tub. His vital signs are within normal limits.

The lesion transilluminates well, and no inguinal nodes are palpable. There is no history of trauma. Findings from a testicular scan are normal. A 15-year-old male presents to the office with the complaint of painless swelling in the left testicle that has varied in size over the past several months.

His intertrigo improved, but he then developed bright red, burning and painful nodules around his scrotum (Figure 1). His medications included omeprazole, alprazolam, amlodipine besylate, atenolol, simvastatin, and valsartan. . His medical history included prostate cancer, hypertension, anxiety disorder, hyperlipidemia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and diverticulosis.

Two days ago he developed a moist, nonproductive cough and rapid breathing. Chest examination shows intercostal retractions along with bilateral, diffuse wheezes and expiratory rhonchi. Physical examination shows nasal flaring and rhinorrhea. He attends a large day-care center and has three schoolaged siblings. His illness began with lowgrade fever and copious, clear nasal discharge. He has received all scheduled childhood immunizations. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 101/min, respirations are 38/min, and blood pressure is 85/60 mm Hg. A 10-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 4-day history of fever and cough.

A 29-year-old woman is prescribed carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia. She has a strong family history of osteoporosis. As a result, the physician also advises her to increase her intake of vitamin D.

His tumor cells contain a point mutation in the p53 gene (TP53), leading to an inactive gene product. A 57-year-old man receives radiation therapy for a squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. Despite therapy, the tumor progressively increases in size, and he dies 6 months later.

An 87-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her son because of progressive memory loss over the past 2 years. Her son says that she repeats herself frequently and has been forgetting to take her routine medications. Mini-Mental State Examination score is 23/30. A CT scan of the head shows mild volume loss. Physical examination is within normal limits for her age. Laboratory studies, including serum vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin), thyroxine (T4), and thyroid-stimulating hormone concentrations, are within normal limits. Her blood pressure is 138/78 mm Hg. She takes hydrochlorothiazide for mild systolic hypertension and levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. She had vulvar cancer 10 years ago treated with wide excision.
Examination of the stillborn shows the absence of a urethral opening. The pregnancy was complicated by oligohydramnios. A male stillborn is delivered at 32 weeks' gestation to a 30-year-old woman.

The woman has a minimally decreased hemoglobin concentration. Genetic studies show a single gene deletion. A couple comes for preconceptional genetic counseling because they both have a family history of α-thalassemia. The man has microcytic anemia and a two-gene deletion.

Urine dipstick shows leukocyte esterase; urinalysis shows WBCs and rare gram-negative rods. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), and blood pressure is 108/60 mm Hg. A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 12 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a prenatal visit. Pregnancy and delivery of her first child were uncomplicated. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 12-week gestation. She feels well. Medications include folic acid and a multivitamin.

Her 16-year-old brother has required two operations for a severe rotator cuff injury he sustained while taking a shower, and she has a maternal cousin who died of a ruptured aortic aneurysm at the age of 26 years. She has had increasingly frequent chest pain with exertion since starting a soccer program 3 months ago. A midsystolic click is heard at the apex. The joints of the upper and lower extremities are hypermobile, including 25 degrees of genu recurvatum, thumbs that may be extended to touch the forearms, and flexibility at the waist, with palms easily touching the floor with straight knees. She is at the 99th percentile for height and 50th percentile for weight. Today, the patient walks with a limp. She has been wearing glasses for 2 years. A 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents for evaluation of recurrent injuries. She usually has pain or swelling of her knees or ankles after practice. The left ankle is swollen and tender; range of motion is limited by pain. Her parents say that she started walking at the age of 14 months and since then has always seemed clumsier and had more injuries than other children.

The pain extends from the epigastrium to the right upper quadrant and is sometimes felt in the right scapula; it lasts about 30 minutes and is not relieved by antacids. A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an 8-week history of intermittent nausea and abdominal pain that occurs 20 to 30 minutes after eating. Examination shows no other abnormalities. She is currently asymptomatic. The last episode occurred after she ate a hamburger and french fries. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 104 kg (230 lb); BMI is 38 kg/m2 . She has not had vomiting.

A 22-year-old male presents to the office with a 5-day history of diarrhea after completing his third course of antibiotics for mastoiditis. Culture on hektoen enteric agar is positive. Physical examination reveals vague generalized abdominal pain on palpation.

Physical examination revealed annular red plaques with scale and superficial erosions over the trunk and extremities. On the lower limbs, infiltrated plaques with prominent crusts were seen (Figure, B). A previously healthy man in his 30s was referred to our department for evaluation of asymptomatic cutaneous lesions that had been present for 4 months. He had been treated with a course of high-potency topical corticosteroids without any improvement. Also, there were papulosquamous lesions on the left sole, but the palms were spared. Strikingly, plaques on both arms showed a corymbiform pattern, with a central and multiple satellite lesions (Figure, A). There was neither regional lymph node enlargement nor systemic involvement. Two biopsy specimens from both types of lesions were obtained for histopathologic evaluation, showing an identical histologic pattern (Figure, C and D). The genital area was not involved. .

Examination reveals an erythematous, fluctuant, elevated mass with 3 midline pores. A 15-year-old male is brought to the office with a 2-day history of painful swelling over the sacral prominence that began after a fall during a high school wrestling match. The patient has a low-grade fever. Rectal examination reveals no induration or pain.

She says, "No, I want to die at home." You are visiting an 86-year-old woman in her home at the request of the patient's daughter because of worsening shortness of breath at rest for the past 2 days. The patient is confined to her home because of severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with cor pulmonale. At that time, both the patient and her daughter signed an addendum to that effect on the patient's advance directive. During the discussion, the patient said, "I'd rather die than be intubated again." Pulse oximetry shows an oxygen saturation of 84% while the patient is breathing 4 L of oxygen. Her daughter takes you aside and says, "My mother doesn't know what she's saying. She was discharged 1 week ago from the hospital following 3 weeks of treatment for pneumonia that required intubation; her hospital stay was complicated by sepsis. Today, the patient is dyspneic and is unable to complete a sentence. Vital signs are temperature 37.8°C (100.0°F), pulse 88/min, respirations 35/min, and blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg. She had a prolonged weaning program from intubation. Prior to discharge, the patient and her daughter met with you to review the patient's advance directive. You ask the patient if she wishes to return to the hospital.

There is tenderness to palpation over the left cheek and no transillumination over the left maxillary sinus. A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of throbbing facial pain. Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F). She does not smoke. The lungs are clear to auscultation. She has a history of recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, sinusitis, and pancreatitis. She has thick nasal secretions. Her vital signs are within normal limits. A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of abdominal pain. Physical examination shows epigastric tenderness.

Examination shows profuse diaphoresis and muscle rigidity. His leukocyte count is 15,600/mm3 , and serum creatine kinase activity is 943 U/L.
